This study introduces a new class of model termed the TVPAM(p, q), representing a zero-mean, temporally evolving Poisson autoregressive process of orders p and q with time-dependent coefficients. We establish sufficient conditions ensuring that the first- and second-order moments remain uniformly bounded across time. Furthermore, we introduce a method to assess the stationarity of the TVPAM(p, q) model and outline estimation techniques for its temporally varying parameters. The practical utility of this approach is demonstrated through the analysis of daily call volumes at a specific New York City fire station. Additionally, we develop a simplified, fixed-coefficient variant of the TVPAM(p, q) for forecasting daily call volumes on unspecified future days. The theoretical findings regarding moment boundedness and parameter stationarity are validated via numerical experiments. Ultimately, the results indicate that the call volume data at the target fire station aligns more closely with the predictions of the temporally varying coefficient model than those of the optimized fixed-coefficient model. Ultimately, this work presents a data-driven framework for modeling and forecasting zero-inflated count data using a seasonal, temporally varying Poisson autoregressive model. Such a framework holds significant value for public safety agencies, as it offers actionable insights into the temporal dynamics of 911 call volumes and supports the development of optimized emergency response strategies. Ultimately, this research also contributes to the broader field of operations research by addressing the challenge of designing efficient response plans for natural disasters and public safety events under conditions of uncertainty. To achieve this, the authors propose a multi-objective mixed-integer linear programming model aimed at optimizing the deployment of first responders during disasters or large-scale emergencies. Ultimately, numerical experiments are used to evaluate the proposed methodology and multi-phase optimization model, while a real-world case study illustrates how public safety agencies can leverage the temporal-variable Poisson autoregressive model and multi-objective optimization framework to create optimized response plans for disasters and mass emergencies. Ultimately, this study also examines the impact of social media on terrorist attacks, defining such attacks as purposeful violence by non-state actors targeting civilians to instill fear and advance political, religious, or ideological goals. The research analyzes the effects of Twitter usage before and after attacks, hypothesizing that terrorists leverage the platform for communication, recruitment, and propaganda. This study introduces a method for estimating planetary atmospheres and sources of light leakage in exoplanet spectroscopy by adapting the technique used to derive exoplanet atmospheres from stellar variability. This approach, termed \textit{photometric leakage}, offers an independent means of characterizing planet spectra, particularly in the infrared where spectroscopic blocking causes flux losses that are difficult to correct. By employing both the \textit{photometric leakage} and a standard correction for atmospheric absorption, we achieve highly accurate planetary flux corrections. When applied to the K2 light curve of HD 99109, this dual correction yields a significant improvement in the fit of the planet's light curve, enabling the derivation of a more precise atmospheric solution. Furthermore, utilizing the correction for atmospheric absorption alongside the residual light curve from the \textit{photometric leakage} correction allows for the analysis of stellar variability. The results from this final step align well with the combined corrections for atmospheric and leakage effects, confirming the validity of this framework. We anticipate that this methodology will be valuable for refining the spectroscopic corrections required for HD 99109 B's atmosphere and for similar systems, such as those investigated by \cite{barman15} and \cite{barman16}. The code implementing this method is accessible at https://github.com/robinbarman/PhotometricLeakage. This paper demonstrates that the Langevin Dynamics (LD) algorithm serves as a reliable and potent method for sampling the conformational space of molecules. We provide a detailed description of the LD algorithm and its implementation within the OpenMM molecular dynamics simulator. Furthermore, we validate the efficacy of LD by comparing it with simulated annealing, molecular dynamics, and the stochastic gradient descent-based MNNetConf sampler across a range of molecules. Our results indicate that LD outperforms these alternative techniques, particularly for complex molecules with extensive conformational spaces, such as retinol and $\alpha$-tocopherol. To facilitate broader application, we have made both the source code and a collection of test molecules available at https://github.com/KristianGentz/LDTests. This study investigates how to leverage human-written image descriptions to evaluate automated systems, a task known as extraction-based evaluation. Unlike traditional approach-based methods, which often fail to capture the semantic nuances of natural language, our proposed framework relies on a neural semantic similarity model. We hypothesize that this model can effectively assess the semantic alignment between an image and its description, even when no matching human-written description is available. To validate this, we conducted experiments on two datasets: Flickr8A and Flickr30A. The results confirm that our framework yields outcomes comparable to existing methods, supporting the conclusion that a neural-based semantic similarity model can successfully evaluate the image–description pairs in these datasets. Furthermore, the findings indicate that our approach performs as well as, if not better than, conventional methods. These results suggest that our framework can serve as a valuable resource for enhancing image description generation, particularly in scenarios where human reference data is scarce. To facilitate this, we have made the source code and trained models publicly accessible at https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/Neural-Semantic-Similarity-for-Evaluating-Image-Descriptions. Ultimately, this work offers a practical solution for automatically evaluating image descriptions, potentially aiding the development of more accurate systems for generating such content. Additionally, the proposed framework could be applied to other extraction-based evaluation challenges, including the assessment of image captions and video descriptions.

This study introduces a geometric field theory derived from the Euler-Arnold equation, which governs the evolution of rigid body angular velocity. By extending this equation to a manifold of Riemannian metrics, a corresponding action principle is formulated. Unlike the standard formulation that utilizes angular velocity, this research focuses on the Riemannian metric itself as the primary variable. Consequently, a novel field theory emerges, characterized by a specific geometric structure. It is demonstrated that this structure aligns with the recently developed symplectic geometry of optimal mass transport. Furthermore, the classical Liouville 1-form is shown to be compatible with this geometry, yielding a symplectic geometry on the manifold of metrics that corresponds to the Euler-Arnold equation. Additionally, a recently identified "exotic" geometry on this manifold is found to be compatible with a bi-Hamiltonian structure for the equation. Finally, an action principle is developed that accommodates this exotic geometry as well.

This study presents a novel approach to predicting the baryon and meson contents of atomic nuclei, grounded in the concept of parton saturation. The predictions rely solely on empirical data regarding the baryon and meson composition of free nucleons and their nuclear modifications, without requiring input from specific baryon or meson production mechanisms. The findings indicate that, for a gold nucleus, the baryon and meson spectra at central collisions are approximately 1.5 times greater than those of a single gold nucleon. These spectra align closely with the baryon and meson fluxes responsible for producing open charm, multi-charmed, and exotic particles. Consequently, this method offers a straightforward technique for estimating baryon and meson fluxes between colliding nuclei, applicable to both existing and future experiments. Furthermore, the approach can be extended to calculate the in-medium lifetimes of heavy mesons and exotic states within nuclei, potentially revealing that certain multi-strange baryons and charmonium exotic states possess in-medium lifetimes comparable to the duration of heavy-ion collisions. This implies that the formation and decay of these particles occur dynamically within the collision environment, rather than solely through production and decay between passing nuclei. Ultimately, this technique provides a mechanism for determining the yield of any particle or exotic state from baryon or meson fluxes, based on the hypothesis that their production arises from gluon hard scattering between these fluxes. Such a method could be utilized to derive yields for various particles and exotic states in future experiments, potentially identifying species with non-zero yields that have yet to be observed. Ultimately, this paper serves as a theoretical work, and the proposed technique for calculating yields of new particles and exotic states from baryon and meson fluxes could be employed to guide future research. Additionally, a companion article details how to apply this method to determine the yield of a specific particle or exotic state, alongside an assessment of the validity of the underlying assumptions. This paper introduces simplified broadband models for integrated data and power wireless systems, moving away from the multi-carrier OFDM approach used in this work and in current industry standards. These models enable the derivation of optimal linear transmission strategies to maximize system capacity. The derived solutions are computationally efficient, requiring only the calculation of eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a positive semi-definite matrix. These results offer valuable insights into system design and establish performance benchmarks for non-linear integer programming approaches aimed at enhancing data rates via beamforming. Equivalence demonstrations between the broadband model and a specific multi-carrier model are provided for both single-user point-to-point (open access) and single-user point-to-point (private access) systems, as illustrated in Figure 1. While the equivalence for the former is exact, it holds approximately for the latter. Extending these equivalences to multi-user point-to-point systems is challenging due to the complexity of user scheduling; however, for a fixed scheduling decision in the multi-carrier domain, an exact equivalence between their broadband counterparts can be achieved. Furthermore, these models can be applied to systems with multiple power amplifiers, a scenario explored in Section VI. The specific broadband model utilized in this section is a simplified version of the single-radio described earlier, constructed by concatenating the impulse responses of all radio's filters (depicted in Figure 5) to form a single effective filter. Additionally, future systems utilizing multiple access methods, such as combining OFDM with discrete multi-tone (DMT) or orthogonal variable spreading factor orthogonal code division multiple access (OVSF-CDMA), can leverage these models. For instance, in a single radio system with multiple DMT users, the multi-carrier problem can first be converted into a single-carrier linear optimization problem using these models, after which optimal solutions for the broadband model's filter coefficients can be converted into frequency-domain gain allocations for each user and subsequently into time-domain filter coefficients. Finally, these models are particularly useful for analyzing the performance of learning-based solutions, such as deep reinforcement learning, in multi-user point-to-point systems, as these methods typically operate in the end-to-end time-domain impulse response domain without knowledge of the system's specific characteristics. By applying these models to a multi-user point-to-point setup, an optimal linear solution serves as an effective reward function for reinforcement learning algorithms to explore. Ultimately, these models are not limited to the system architecture investigated in this work; they can be adapted to any linear transmit scheme, including non-linear ones. This paper presents a unified framework for adjusting parton distribution function (PDF) models using both direct and indirect measurement techniques. While the TESTFIT code has been employed for the CT18, NNPDF3.1, and MSHT20 collaborations, and the ROOT-based chain method has been used for the same groups plus ABM13, these approaches have operated independently. The framework described here integrates both direct and indirect fitting methodologies within ROOT, rendering the use of TESTFIT unnecessary. Although the primary goal is to create a unified system for existing groups, the approach is general enough to accommodate future projects. The fitting workflow is managed by a dedicated theory code that generates input files for the MCFM direct estimator and TESTFIT for its estimators. These estimators are linked via external scripts, which also coordinate the execution of TESTFIT and the generation of output files by the theory code for the subsequent iteration step. By combining all direct and indirect estimators into a single environment, this framework eliminates the need for external code like TESTFIT or specific rootles scripts during the iteration process. Consequently, the entire fitting chain can be executed using only standard Linux and ROOT environments. The efficacy of this framework is demonstrated through the CT18 part 2 fitting process. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/MEWGAN/PDFAdjustmentFramework.

This study employs a linearized structural model to investigate how acoustic excitations influence an excited jet fire reaction, aiming to reduce structural loads. The research begins with a linearized structural model derived from a linearized Eulerian Navier-Stokes/structural model, designed to assess the impact of both longitudinal and transverse excitations on the flame and structure. Subsequently, an active flame methodology is introduced to generate linearly stable longitudinal and transverse acoustic modes, which are superimposed onto the linearized structure model. The results indicate that the flame responds to excitation by oscillating, which alters the heat flux distribution across the impinging structure. Furthermore, the findings reveal that the structure deforms in response to acoustic excitations, causing the linearized structural model to deviate from linearity. Finally, the study examines the combined effects of heat flux variations and structural deformations on the loads experienced by the structure.

Nonlocal gravity (NLG) represents a nonlocal extension of Einstein's gravitational theory, formulated through a constitutive approach analogous to that used in nonlocal elasticity. In this framework, the constitutive relation is expressed via a kernel kernel that connects current field values to their historical states. This kernel operates within the multiplicative group of special tetrads, which function as the affine connection in this theory. Specifically, a nonlocal affine connection is derived from a nonlocal tetrad kernel. This paper offers a detailed examination of the constitutive connection within NLG, with the goal of establishing a consistent and viable theory. Initially, we outline the fundamental principles of the nonlocal tetrad and affine connection. Subsequently, we introduce a hierarchy of nonlocal tetrad kernels, defining a corresponding hierarchy of nonlocal affine connections. We then analyze the characteristics of this kernel, focusing on its matrix structure, symmetry, and invariance properties. Finally, we present a novel definition of the metric tensor as a function of the nonlocal tetrad kernel and its inverse, thereby formulating a nonlocal version of the field equations. To conclude, we propose a constitutive model for the nonlocal tetrad kernel and its inverse, derived from a linear operator acting on a linear nonlocal strain tensor. This model incorporates a single hereditary kernel, which in turn defines a linear nonlocal affine connection. The feasibility of this model is demonstrated through the derivation of a linear operator that links the nonlocal Riemann tensor to its local counterpart. Additionally, we derive a linear constitutive relation for the energy-momentum tensor that incorporates a hereditary kernel. As a final step, we establish a modified fractional nonlinear constitutive relation for the special nonlocal tetrad kernel and its inverse, which relies on a fractional hereditary kernel. This establishes a hierarchy of models, all governed by a single hereditary kernel. These models are applied to a point mass to derive its nonlinear nonlocal field equations. The results indicate that a linear hereditary kernel yields a linear energy-momentum constitutive relation, whereas a fractional hereditary kernel produces a nonlinear energy-momentum constitutive relation. Furthermore, a fractional hereditary kernel is required to ensure the positivity of the special nonlocal tetrad kernel's eigenvalues. Ultimately, this study provides a comprehensive analysis of the nonlocal tetrad kernel, its inverse, and the metric tensor, alongside an in-depth review of constitutive models for the nonlocal affine connection and field equations. These investigations are intended to advance the development of constitutive models

Collisions of small systems at high energies, encompassing proton-nucleus, heavy-ion, and proton-proton interactions, represent a significant area of research at the LHC. While heavy-ion collisions have long been the primary focus for investigating Quark-Gluon Plasma formation, the nature of particles produced in proton-proton and proton-nucleus collisions remains an open question. These smaller systems offer an ideal environment to test if collective phenomena occur and to assess the validity of theoretical models used to describe quark and gluon dynamics. This paper provides an overview of collective effects observed across these various small systems, covering both experimental results and theoretical frameworks. It specifically examines flow characteristics in proton-nucleus collisions, strangeness enhancement, and the suppression of high-pT hadrons and photons. The discussion also addresses the influence of centrality, multiplicity, and other relevant variables. Furthermore, the article surveys recent theoretical developments in small systems, including hydrodynamic models, partonic and atomic theories, and hadronization mechanisms. Finally, it highlights remaining challenges and identifies promising directions for future investigation.

We address the potential link between the minimum intervals separating X-ray outburst pairs in Galactic Centre dormant binary systems and their accretion disc properties. Additionally, we examine the interval between outbursts in transient pulsar systems, specifically focusing on the minimum intervals between double outbursts in the neutron star systems XTE J1739-285A and PSR J0205+6451. Regarding these systems, we challenge the conclusion by Casella et al. (arXiv:1907.07293) that the minimum interval in Galactic Centre dormant binaries is governed by the viscous timescale of their discs. We contend that this assertion relies on the prior, yet unproven, assumption of a single outburst mechanism. Furthermore, we dispute the claim by Casella et al. that the interval between double outbursts in X-ray transients is unrelated to their disc characteristics. Ultimately, we propose that the minimum interval between outbursts in both Galactic Centre dormant binaries and neutron star transients is governed by the mass of the associated accretion disc. This conclusion aligns with the observed intervals in various Galactic Centre dormant binaries and the double outbursts in XTE J1739-285A and PSR J0205+6451, without requiring the introduction of a specific outburst mechanism.

This study introduces HyperDegrade, a system that intentionally slows down CPU execution rates to achieve significant energy savings. Unlike existing techniques that rely on underutilized hardware resources, HyperDegrade operates without requiring additional hardware support. The approach consists of two phases: initially, a static analysis phase generates an optimized assembly code schedule; secondly, a runtime phase executes this pre-generated schedule. Evaluation using the SPEC CPU 2006 benchmark suite demonstrates that HyperDegrade enables execution rates up to 20 times slower than native speeds with minimal performance degradation. Compared to prior methods, HyperDegrade delivers superior execution rates at equivalent energy levels, or alternatively, achieves greater energy savings at the same execution rates. These findings indicate that Intentionally Reduced Execution Rates (IRER) remain viable even at extremely low speeds, such as 1/20th of the native rate. Consequently, this work offers a practical solution for extending the operational duration of battery-powered devices and for enabling the execution of computationally intensive tasks on energy-constrained hardware. The open-source implementation of HyperDegrade is accessible at: https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/HyperDegrade.

This paper introduces a new unknotting procedure applicable to both traditional and welded links, which involves pulling straight segments of the diagram and performing crossing changes. While this method has previously been observed empirically, no formal proof existed until now. We establish that this procedure fails for standard knot theory but succeeds for traditional and welded links. Consequently, this technique offers a powerful tool for demonstrating that certain traditional and welded links cannot be equivalent to unknots within their respective frameworks. As a byproduct, we provide concise proofs for two known results: first, that no unknotting sequence of type $R_2$ can exist for the trefoil knot $3_1$; second, that the unknotting number for any traditional or welded link is at least half the difference between its bridge number and two. Furthermore, we define a new invariant for traditional links, termed the unknotting distance, and investigate its properties. The proposed unknotting strategy finds practical application in biology, particularly in analyzing the entanglement of DNA and proteins. Our mathematical findings regarding this procedure and its associated invariants may assist biologists in assessing the level of entanglement in biological chains. Specifically, the new invariants introduced here could serve as a simpler alternative to computing the Alexander module or other invariants required to prove that a specific traditional or welded link diagram can form an unknot via a certain unknotting sequence. To support these concepts visually, we have developed an open-source Java application called UnknotIt, available at http://topology.at.ua.edu/UnknotIt/. This program enables users to implement the unknotting procedure on traditional and welded link diagrams and offers a user-friendly environment for exploring the invariants defined in this article. The ConceiJo software is also utilized in this work.

This study introduces a real-time tactical game designed to evaluate how multi-agent systems collaborate within the limits of their computational power and communication capabilities. Unlike previous research that assumes ideal communication conditions, this game operates on a conventional network where the quality of links between agents is both random and dynamic. To address the challenge of learning optimal strategies under these unpredictable communication constraints, we developed a novel learning algorithm. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that this algorithm successfully enables the acquisition of an approximately optimal policy. Furthermore, the simulations provide evidence that an agent's rationality—specifically its tendency to act fairly and honestly—can be effectively learned. These findings hold significant implications for the development of intelligent systems deployed in real-world tactical environments. The source code for this project is accessible at https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/TaCoC.

This paper introduces a Cartesian decomposition approach to embed a group acting on a simply connected geodesic space $X$ (with curvature bounded above by 1) into a product of Garland spaces. This extends the author's earlier work, which specifically addressed groups acting on trees. As a primary application, the embedding technique yields new findings regarding fixed point properties and property (T). Additionally, the method provides fresh proofs of previously established embedding results for groups acting on trees and buildings. The proposed Cartesian decomposition strategy may also be applicable to other contexts involving embeddings into product spaces. Furthermore, this article serves as a self-contained guide to various group embedding methods, summarizing existing techniques and highlighting their interconnections.

Collaborations like LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA are constructing laser interferometric gravitational wave detectors operating in a Michelson-sagnac hybrid configuration to maximize sensitivity. This setup represents a compromise aimed at achieving broad-band sensitivity, yet it results in significant sensitivity drops at both low and high frequencies. The frequency-dependent losses at low frequencies are well understood and addressed with active seismic isolation and sensor-based feedback control. Conversely, the high-frequency sensitivity degradation, caused by the finite travel time of light within the interferometer, has not been fully investigated. In this study, we introduce a new interferometric topology called sloshing-Sagnac for both Michelson and triangular topologies that effectively mitigates high-frequency sensitivity degradation. Utilizing matrix formalism, we demonstrate that the sloshing-Sagnac configuration offers high-frequency sensitivity comparable to its low-frequency band, contingent upon appropriate arm length selection. Given that gravitational waves in the 200+ Hz range are of prime interest for future stochastic background searches and transient events, this configuration could significantly enhance science-driven sensitivity. Furthermore, we anticipate that the sloshing-Sagnac topology will yield unexpected benefits for waveform parameter estimation and stochastic background searches. Our analysis confirms that the sloshing-Sagnac topology can improve gravitational wave sensitivity at high frequencies by an order of magnitude without requiring modifications to existing detectors. Implementing this topology in detectors could also provide a novel testbed for probing light's behavior in non-inertial frames and exploring equivalence principle violations via interferometric sensors. To enable this, we must develop new optical components and topologies, as current detectors lack the necessary elements. We outline a feasible path to realize this topology in current detectors and explore its potential applications. While the sloshing-Sagnac topology holds promise for enhancing high-frequency sensitivity in gravitational wave detectors, other factors such as low-frequency sensitivity, thermal noise, and seismic noise must also be considered for optimal overall sensitivity. Additionally, distinguishing between the fundamental sloshing-Sagnac topology and the triplex topology (employed in the TriPLEx experiment) is crucial, as they are distinct configurations. Finally, the sloshing-Sagnac topology could find utility in other fields, including seismology, acoustic sensing, and inertial sensing, where similar challenges exist. This paper addresses the non-intersecting visibility area challenge within the XL-MIMO stochastic access protocol. First, we establish the system model and formulate the optimization problem aimed at maximizing total visibility. Second, we propose a two-stage algorithm: initially, optimal serving access points are selected for each user equipment, followed by the determination of non-intersecting visibility regions for all access points. Extensive simulations demonstrate that our proposed algorithm effectively maximizes total visibility and achieves significant improvements compared to existing methods. Furthermore, the simulation results validate the effectiveness of our two-stage approach in optimizing non-intersecting visibility areas for XL-MIMO stochastic protocols. Finally, the practical implications of these findings are discussed. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/Non-IntersectingVisibilityAreas.

Although recent advances in language modeling and generation have predominantly relied on neural networks, these models often fail to achieve high accuracy on test sets compared to the significant improvements seen in linguistic tasks like prediction. This discrepancy suggests that neural networks still struggle to capture certain linguistic characteristics. In this study, we propose a hybrid approach for both modeling and creation that integrates an $n$-gram component with a deep network. By assigning the $n$-gram module the responsibility of handling specific linguistic features, the deep network can focus on other aspects through a residual learning strategy. Experimental results demonstrate that this hybrid framework outperforms both pure $n$-gram and purely neural models in terms of accuracy. Furthermore, when applied to generation, our method surpasses previous state-of-the-art techniques, and qualitative analyses confirm that the approach effectively leverages the strengths of both components. To facilitate future research, we have open-sourced our code and pre-trained weights at https://github.com/yutaka2018/Ngram-Res-Transformer. Specifically, integrating the $M_3$ trigram table from the CMU toolkit with the BERT base uncased model yielded the following accuracies: 83.33\% for Byte Pair Encoding (BPE), 83.29\% for Context Language Modeling (CtxLM), and 83.25\% for the Residual Transformer (ResTrans). Similarly, combining the $M_4$ four-gram table from the CMU toolkit with the TinyBERT global model (global = true) produced these results: 82.91\% for BPE, 82.88\% for CtxLM, and 82.84\% for ResTrans. Using the $M_5$ five-gram table from the CMU toolkit alongside the DistilBERT base model resulted in: 82.77\% for BPE, 82.74\% for CtxLM, and 82.71\% for ResTrans. Finally, employing the $M_6$ six-gram table from the CMU toolkit with the LightBERT base model achieved: 82.66\% for BPE, 82.63\% for CtxLM, and 82.60\% for ResTrans.

This study introduces Informed OCR (iOCR), a specialized system designed to enhance the accuracy of conventional OCR when processing images of handwritten text. The proposed framework consists of two phases: during training, a dictionary learning algorithm generates a vocabulary of symbol representations from sample images, while in the operational phase, a Bayesian classifier selects the most probable symbol for each image region using the learned representations. Experiments conducted with standard OCR on images of ballot cards from the 2016 Indian general election demonstrate that iOCR achieves higher accuracy than traditional methods. The source code and datasets are accessible at https://github.com/rajat1997/iOCR. Distinct from conventional approaches, this solution does not require manual correction of errors by human operators. The detailed description of this framework is presented in Section 2. Figure 1 illustrates the workflow: (a) shows a zoomed-in image of a ballot card with a handwritten vote for the Independent party, (b) displays the corresponding output from traditional OCR, and (c) presents the improved result from the proposed method.

This study examines global atmospheric circulation patterns in the planets of our Solar System using a simplified two-dimensional general circulation model. The model incorporates Coriolis forces, centrifugal forces, gravity, friction, and radiative cooling, while convection is included via a simple parameterization. It features a simplified energy balance and moisture balance, along with a simplified cloud radiative feedback mechanism. By analyzing circulation patterns across different planets, the model successfully reproduces key features such as the transition from geostrophic to cyclostrophic balance, the formation of super-rotating atmospheres, the number and latitude of jets and storms, and the development of cloud bands. These results are achieved without adjusting friction coefficients for each planet and with a single cloud radiative feedback coefficient applicable to all. The findings indicate that centrifugal force, cyclostrophic balance, and cloud radiative feedback are essential for accurately simulating the atmospheric circulations of the outer planets. Furthermore, the results support the hypothesis that planetary Coriolis forces, rather than atmospheric mass, primarily determine the number of jets and storms. Detailed investigations into circulation patterns reveal how cyclostrophic and geostrophic balances interact with friction and radiative cooling to generate distinct atmospheric features. Additionally, the study identifies specific atmospheric conditions required for the emergence of super-rotating atmospheres. Ultimately, this simple model offers valuable insights into the physical mechanisms driving the circulation patterns of outer planetary atmospheres, potentially aiding in the interpretation of atmospheric data from extrasolar planets. A complementary report will explore the atmospheric structures of gaseous giant exoplanets with masses ranging from Jupiter to Brown Dwarfs. Ultimately, this work aims to clarify the circulation patterns observed in these extrasolar gaseous giant planets and brown dwarfs through the lens of both cyclostrophic and geostrophic balances. To facilitate these investigations, an open-source code has been developed for this simplified global circulation model, which can be downloaded from https://github.com/robertlede/Comparative_atmospheric_circulation. This study introduces a novel integral representation for the regularized inverse Gamma function, derived by applying a sequence of transformations to an existing integral form of the Gamma function. Leveraging this new expression, we formulate an integral definition for the reciprocal Gamma function that accommodates all complex values, thereby generalizing the previously established regularized integral. These generalized integral forms of both the Gamma and its reciprocal are anticipated to prove valuable in specific applications. Furthermore, we derive a connection between our regularized integral of the reciprocal Gamma function and a recently proposed integral definition by Srivastava et al., which operates within the sector $|\arg(z)| < \pi - \epsilon$. Finally, we establish a relationship linking our regularized integral of the Gamma function to a recent regularization method introduced by Manoukian. The corresponding integral expressions for these functions are examined in detail.

We introduce a novel hydrodynamic framework for classical and quantum fluids, termed random hydrodynamics, by extending the methods used to derive kinetic theories from microscopic theories. Specifically, we generalize the derivation of the Boltzmann equation from both classical and quantum Boltzmann-Liouville (or Vlasov) equations, and from classical and Bose-Einstein (BE) kinetic theories, to a derivation of hydrodynamics directly from the classical and BE phase-space representations. This approach yields a hydrodynamic theory that incorporates quantum effects and stochastic fluctuations both spatially and temporally, analogous to how the Boltzmann theory accounts for non-equilibrium phenomena and fluctuations when going beyond equilibrium hydrodynamics. Similar to the hierarchy of kinetic theories, this new hierarchy of stochastic hydrodynamic theories for classical and quantum fluids is systematically closed by the order of gradients and stochastic fluctuations. We focus on the classical and quantum stochastic hydrodynamic extensions of the BE equilibrium distribution and its associated fluctuations. The resulting theory, which we call the Phase-Space Random Quantum Hydrodynamics (PRQH), offers a fresh perspective on the microscopic origins of hydrodynamic modes and fluctuations in quantum fluids. It serves as a valuable tool for identifying quantum effects in experiments and simulations, particularly in ultra-cold gases, and can be employed as a practical method for simulating these systems.

Structured test metrics play a crucial role in enhancing neural machine translation and generating actionable feedback for linguistic systems. This study introduces a rigorous, precise evaluation method for these metrics using the standard family of pairwise evaluation measures. The proposed framework, Precise Paired-Permutation Examination (P3), systematically assesses how ranking-based methods like human evaluation, Matthews correlation, and Spearman correlation align with structured metrics such as BLEU, Meteor, and MACHEC to derive a comprehensive precision score. The results indicate that for most metric/human evaluation combinations, precision drops significantly when human evaluations follow a specific sequence: R1>R2>R3>R4, where R4 represents a contradiction to R3 (for instance, A>B>C>D>A), and R3 is at least as good as R2, which is at least as good as R1. These findings suggest that existing pairwise methods and structured metrics effectively identify when a translation improves over a reference but fail to capture the specific nature of those improvements. Conversely, when a metric contradicts human judgments regarding the ordering of pairs, the precision score typically remains high, indicating that the contradiction is primarily due to the human evaluation not preferring the pair the metric ranks higher. Ultimately, this work demonstrates that current structured metrics do not offer the precision required for a fully precise evaluation of neural systems, and the traditional assumption that a combination of a structured metric and a sample-size-weighted human evaluation (MATH) is sufficient for evaluating neural systems needs to be reconsidered. This study addresses the underutilized issue of bias in derived data, specifically concerning solar vector magnetic field measurements. We first demonstrate that existing analyses have overlooked derived data bias, which can be amplified by noise and outliers. Furthermore, we reveal that current solar vector magnetograph instruments are susceptible to bias due to the inversion of noisy linear polarization signals in regions with weak magnetic fields. To tackle this, we propose a novel framework for identifying and mitigating such bias, which relies solely on the linear and circular polarization data and the physical properties of the solar atmosphere, requiring no additional assumptions about the inversion algorithm. Finally, we offer guidelines for reducing noise and minimizing outliers in vector magnetic field data. For any finite classical group $G$ acting on a vector space $V$, we define and examine the lattice $\mathcal{B}(G)$ consisting of subspace sets that are both closed under complementation by an inversion and ordered by inclusion. Furthermore, we establish a correspondence between specific Birkhoff characters of $\mathcal{B}(G)$ and the collection of irreducible rational characters of $G$. Applying this framework, we derive the explicit boolean structure for the symplectic group $Sp_{4}(2)$. Our analysis reveals that for classical groups, this structure is generally not atomic; specifically, we identify an infinite family of simple groups that reside within the boolean structure of an invertible classical group yet remain outside its atomic structure. Additionally, we observe that for the symplectic group $Sp_{4}(q)$, the boolean structure is isomorphic to that of a product of two invariant subspace lattices. Finally, we conjecture a similar isomorphism for the orthogonal groups $O_{2n}(q)$. These findings offer a novel perspective on invertible classical groups, potentially aiding in the investigation of their character theory. Alongside this classification, the intrinsic equations for both regular slant helix and regular circulant helix curves are derived. We introduce the ATOMIC project, aimed at constructing an atlas of machine common knowledge to enable robots perform If-Then reasoning. This project encompasses a suite of tools and resources designed to systematize and share common sense knowledge regarding atomic actions and their prerequisites within a first-order logic framework. These resources facilitate the creation of If-Then inference engines for various natural language systems, allowing a robot to anticipate the conditions necessary to execute an action described in the antecedent. Although this approach does not replace the immediate determination of action feasibility from the current context, it offers an effective means for a robot to infer such details from textual descriptions of contexts, for instance, when reading a narrative. To illustrate these capabilities, we developed a set of natural language inference tasks based on movie plots, which are detailed herein. Furthermore, we outline how this atlas of common sense knowledge can support other systems, including those responsible for grounding actions and their context descriptions into first-order logic. To make this atlas as comprehensive as possible, we developed a specialized natural language for specifying common sense facts, termed ATOMIC-SentenceFile (ATOMIC-SF). This study introduces a novel end-to-end method for multi-view video forecasting, addressing the challenge with a fresh framework. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on conditional generative models, our technique employs a neural architecture designed to learn a dual representation of video frames, enabling the prediction of unseen views from a single input frame. We formulated this problem as a multi-task learning challenge, utilizing a collection of pairs consisting of one static image and its corresponding two video sequences from different angles. The architecture comprises two modules: a shared layer responsible for generating the dual representation of the input image and predicting the future video, and a view-specific module that converts the image and future video into fixed-dimensional vectors. Extensive experiments were conducted on both synthetic and real-world datasets to evaluate the proposed method. The results demonstrate that this approach effectively learns to predict videos from unseen angles based on a single input frame and outperforms current state-of-the-end methods on both real and synthetic datasets. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/DRief.

This study introduces a novel framework for heart sound categorization that tackles additive interference and non-linear distortions arising from sensor movement. The proposed method comprises two sequential stages. Initially, a deformable network compensates for non-linear distortions caused by sensor displacement prior to addressing additive noise. In the second stage, an additive noise countermeasure is applied to classify heart sounds. The first countermeasure involves a convolutional layer designed to eliminate background noise, followed by a categorical classifier. The second involves a specialized additive noise countermeasure layer, also followed by a categorical classifier. Experimental results demonstrate that this two-stage approach surpasses existing methods, including end-to-end solutions. Specifically, the proposed framework achieved an accuracy of 98.1%, representing a 1.1% improvement over the second-highest performing method. These findings confirm the efficacy of the proposed approach in mitigating both linear and non-linear noise issues. Ultimately, this work offers a new solution for heart sound categorization that effectively manages sensor movement-induced distortions and background interference. Potential applications span fetal heart sound monitoring, cardiac auscultation, and automated analysis of heart sounds. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/AbdulrahmanAlshammari/ConDeformNet.

This study investigates the underluminosity of specific carbon monoline emissions relative to the $J=1\rightarrow0$ transition within the molecular gas reservoirs of galaxies. We find that the subthermal excitation of certain lines is a widespread phenomenon, particularly affecting the C\,ii $2\rightarrow1$ and $1\rightarrow0$ transitions as well as the HC\,n $1\rightarrow0$ and $2\rightarrow1$ lines for $n\geq1$. To address the difficulties in modeling these reservoirs due to the coexistence of multiple carbon monoline emissions, we developed a simplified two-level system model. This approach enables the derivation of the total molecular gas mass ($\rm M_{H_2}$) and the specific energy density ($\rho_{\rm tot}$) directly from the integrated fluxes of the A\,ii $1\rightarrow0$ and C\,ii $2\rightarrow1$ lines. Utilizing a sample of 1,000 local galaxies, we confirm a strong correlation between the integrated flux ratio of the C\,ii $2\rightarrow1$ to $1\rightarrow0$ lines and both $\rm M_{H_2}$ and SFR, which allows for the estimation of gas fraction ($\rm f_{gas}$) and specific SFR ($\rm sSFR$). Furthermore, we demonstrate that the product of $\rm M_{H_2}$ and $\rho_{\rm tot}$ aligns closely with the total volumetric star formation rate ($\rm V.SFR_{tot}$). Based on the principles of detailed balance and radiative transfer, we conclude that the underluminosity of the C\,ii $1\rightarrow0$ and HC\,n ($n\geq1$) lines arises from the saturation of the total optical depth ($\tau_{\rm tot}$) in the resonant scattering of the C\,ii $2\rightarrow1$ line. Finally, we highlight the potential utility of the C\,ii $2\rightarrow1$ / $1\rightarrow0$ line ratio as an indicator for identifying the physical conditions of molecular gas reservoirs. It remains uncertain whether a starburst occurs in the most massive galaxies when the transition in the slope of the main sequence turnover takes place. To investigate this, we examined the potential influence of central feedback from Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) and supernovae (SN) by analyzing the role of bulges. Our findings indicate that the turnover at the highest masses is driven by the rapid decline of star formation within bulges. Furthermore, the slope of this turnover is determined by the proportion of light emitted from the bulge. These results support the conclusion that the turnover at elevated masses is a result of quenching due to central feedback, rather than a sudden onset of a starburst. Consequently, the most massive galaxies are characterized by dominant bulges and low specific star formation rates, a configuration that aligns with the prediction of bottom-up hierarchical assembly. In contrast, the initial slope of the main sequence at lower masses is governed by the balance between gas supply and feedback; specifically, the turnover from the "blue" to the "red" main sequence at 10.5 $\sun$ per decade is caused by the steepening of the molecular gas main sequence. These results collectively support a formation model where the most massive galaxies assemble through major mergers of galaxies with comparable masses, a process that facilitates bulge growth and triggers the turnover at those extreme masses. This study also highlights the utility of bulge analysis for understanding galaxy evolution and emphasizes the necessity of accurately measuring bulge properties, a task for which we developed an automated method. Ultimately, our results suggest that the most massive galaxies are essentially "failed" ultra-massive galaxies from the early universe, where the turnover resulted from a shift in the dominant feedback mechanism from AGN to supernovae. Given that the star forming main sequence exhibits a bimodal distribution at masses above $10^{10.5} M_{\sun}$, we propose that the two resulting populations—the classical main sequence and the turnover trace—are not fundamentally different, but rather represent galaxies with varying bulge fractions at a specific epoch. To effectively test this hypothesis, deeper observations are required to precisely determine bulge fractions across cosmic time. Such data could be provided by the JWRF "BulgeDriven" program, for which we have developed a technique to derive bulge fractions directly from spectral energy distributions. This study presents a cross-language sentiment analysis system designed to predict the sentiment of Serbian texts based on their English counterparts. The objective is to enable the moderation of Serbian user comments on social media by leveraging existing automated English moderation tools. The proposed framework employs a multi-task learning architecture where a Serbian text classifier and an English classifier operate jointly. Additionally, the system incorporates a cross-language mapping module responsible for generating semantic representations of Serbian sentences. These representations are then utilized by the English classifier to perform sentiment prediction. Experimental results demonstrate that the multi-task model outperforms both a unimodal Serbian classifier and a baseline cross-language system. Furthermore, the findings indicate that the introduction of the cross-language task enhances the classification accuracy of the Serbian model, while the semantic representations of the Serbian sentences effectively support sentiment prediction in the target language. We report the detection of a giant planet orbiting the ultra-steady, ultra-fast rotating B0.5IVp star HD 179608. This discovery implies that HD 179608's rotation has been accelerated by the gravitational influence of the planet, mirroring a mechanism previously identified in the $\gamma$2 CV-9 system. However, HD 179608 maintains a significantly higher rotation rate than $\gamma$2 CV-9 despite hosting a more distant planet, suggesting that additional factors beyond simple angular momentum conservation are at work. We evaluate the hypothesis that tidal dissipation in HD 179608 is unusually efficient due to enhanced magnetic braking caused by a strong, rapid rotation-driven stellar wind. Furthermore, we consider the possibility that HD 179608 experienced a recent mass-accretion event from a now-disintegrated planet, which accounted for its current rapid spin. Ultimately, we conclude that the spectroscopic faculae on HD 179608 are likely the result of atmospheric gas being dragged inward by the orbiting planet. This phenomenon offers a valuable natural laboratory for investigating the interaction between giant planets and their host stars, with implications for the spin-up processes observed in close-in exoplanets. Such interactions also play a crucial role in the evolution of compact X-ray and gamma-ray binary systems, as well as the formation of millisecond pulsars. The detected planet has been designated HD 179608 b, and the data supporting this finding are made available via the Exoplanet Archive at http://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/. The source code for this study can be accessed at https://github.com/robinoliver/SpinUpFacade.

Fake news spreads rapidly through social media, endangering public safety. While deep learning methods have been effective at identifying counterfeit news from existing articles, their application to unseen articles remains limited due to data scarcity. Although this challenge has primarily been addressed using textual data, our approach leverages the complementary strengths of both textual and visual information to create a more effective solution. Specifically, we introduce MetaCVD, a novel framework designed to detect counterfeit videos from previously unseen articles. By combining a meta learning strategy with process modeling, our method enables a model trained solely on structured data to identify fake videos in real-time, even for articles for which no labeled counterfeit video data exists. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MetaCVD significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in detecting counterfeit news. Furthermore, the framework's capabilities are further validated through additional tasks, including few-shot learning and classification. The source code is available at: https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/Multimodal-Emergent-Counterfeit-News-Detection-Via-Meta-Neural-Process-Networks.

Evaluated on two public brain MRI datasets, P-AVAE demonstrates superior performance compared to current approaches, as evidenced by higher semantic effectiveness and reduced classification attack success rates. This paper introduces UniCE, a unified framework for contrastive learning that enables single-model execution across nine distinct attribute extraction tasks. These tasks fall into three categories: classification-based methods, including supervised and few-shot learning; regression-based approaches, covering supervised and few-shot scenarios; and contrastive-based techniques, encompassing both supervised and unsupervised contexts. UniCE integrates these diverse methods into a single architecture, leveraging a shared contrastive learning strategy. By utilizing nine public datasets, the study demonstrates that UniCE not only delivers competitive performance for each task but also significantly outperforms traditional contrastive learning approaches. Furthermore, the research provides empirical evidence confirming the effectiveness of the proposed framework. The source code and datasets are accessible at: https://github.com/ChenYi-98/UniCE.

We introduce a method to enhance pre-trained large language models (LLMs) with domain-specific knowledge without necessitating further training. This approach integrates a lightweight, interpretable skills taxonomy into the model, enabling it to recognize and act upon specific skills within prompts. This taxonomy serves as a structured representation of the skills embedded in the LLM's knowledge, facilitating the identification and invocation of individual skills during inference. Unlike traditional taxonomy learning methods that rely on hierarchical clustering of semantic embeddings, our technique employs a bottom-up strategy to automatically learn a taxonomy from text data suitable for extensive language models. To address the challenge of data volume required for training on an extensive model, we developed a novel sampling algorithm capable of processing massive datasets of natural language interactions. We validated this method on two dialogue datasets: a public dataset of doctor-patient conversations and a private dataset of lawyer-client interactions. The results indicate that this approach yields a more granular taxonomy and produces more accurate skill predictions compared to existing methods. Furthermore, when tested on both datasets, SKILL demonstrated superior performance in detecting and executing skills within given prompts relative to baseline approaches. This work offers a structured insight into how LLMs acquire knowledge from textual data and provides a framework for inferring specific domain skills from dialogue data, which can be applied to train specialized models or verify that models possess required skills. Our code and taxonomy are accessible at https://github.com/IBM/skill-taxonomy.

Non-linear interactions between photons and gravity within the vacuum region of extremal and near-extremal Reissner-Nordström (RN) black holes give rise to non-linear thermodynamic characteristics. This study examines the fractional image formation of extremal and near-extremal non-linear charged AdS black holes, demonstrating that gravitational non-linearities influence optical phenomena. Furthermore, we analyze the connection between optical and thermal characteristics, along with the emergence of phase transitions. The results indicate that gravitational non-linearities can be effectively addressed through a combination of optical and thermal observations. Additionally, we establish that these non-linear effects manifest as apparent charge over-shooting in thermodynamic processes, contrasting with the under-shooting observed in linear models. Finally, we confirm that the impact of non-linear charge on the second-order thermodynamic phase transition is negligible. These findings hold significant implications for future astronomical observations and black hole research. The analysis in this work is based on the geodesic equation, fractional image formation, and the Hawking temperature. Furthermore, the relationship between charge non-linearity and electric field non-linearity is utilized to investigate thermodynamic behaviors and phase transitions.

We introduce a method to visualize entanglement and quantum synchronization within the Wigner-Weyl tomograms of composite quantum systems. Applying this approach to composite harmonic oscillators, we offer a graphical depiction of entanglement and synchronization in their Gaussian tomograms. Furthermore, we demonstrate within these same Gaussian tomograms that certain types of entanglement and synchronization can occur simultaneously. Finally, we present evidence in the non-Gaussian tomograms of a specific class of anisotropic anharmonic oscillators for the coexistence of previously unidentified entanglement forms and synchronization variants. These findings indicate that non-classical correlations and classical-like behaviors can manifest concurrently in composite quantum systems. Additionally, the use of quantum tomograms as a tool for analyzing and identifying various entanglement and synchronization forms is explored. We present an algorithm to construct the submodule lattice of a multiplicity-free module from its Weyl character using the Bernstein-Gelfand-Gelfand (BGG) decomposition line, a technique originally developed by Frenkel, Mukhin, and Stoyanovskii for binomial modules. This approach is particularly valuable when accessing the actual module is challenging. Our construction relies on a specific property of the BGG decomposition line, which we also leverage to define a new invariant: the "coincidence number." This invariant quantifies the extent to which distinct segments of the line appear identical. We establish that the submodule lattice is fully determined by both the BGG decomposition line and the coincidence number of the associated segment. Furthermore, we introduce a method to calculate the coincidence number without requiring knowledge of the underlying module or lattice. As a practical application, we utilize this framework to derive the submodule lattice for a multiplicity-free representation of $\mathfrak{sl}_4$ that features a high number of submodules and for which the segment exhibiting non-trivial coincidences is extensive. Finally, we outline potential directions for future research. This work serves as a companion to the arXiv manuscript titled: The Lattice of Submodules of a Multiplicity Free Module on sl4 with Specific Characteristics.

Subsequently, we investigate minimal and classical hypersurfaces known to fulfill one or more of these biharmonic operator equations. We conclude by posing open questions regarding the recurring biharmonic nature of these hypersurfaces when considered in the context of Sasakian space forms. Additionally, we provide a classification of Biharmonic Hypersurfaces With The Recurring Operators In The Hyperbolic Domain. Throughout this work, we establish new results, derive several important consequences, and offer comprehensive classifications for hypersurfaces with the recurring biharmonic operator in both Euclidean and Hyperbolic domains. A family of graphs $\mathcal{F}$ is termed $p/q$-identifiable if, for any two distinct graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$ drawn from the blow-up of $G_1$ up to order $p$ of some graph $H$ (denoted $HB_1(G_1)$) and the blow-up of $G_1$ up to order $q$ of a potentially different graph $K$ (denoted $HB_1(G_1)$), the fact that $G_1$ admits an isomorphism $\phi$ satisfying $\phi(G_1) \cong \phi(B_1(G_1))$ guarantees that $\mathcal{F}$ is identifiable. This concept extends naturally to graphs, edges, and graphs with specified diameters. It has been established that all families of trees are $1/2$-identifiable, a result generalized herein to $p/q$-identifiability for $p \ge 1$ and $q \ge 2$. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that for $p \ge 1$ and $q \ge 2$, a family consisting of paths and their union is $p/q$-identifiable if and only if its members have a bounded diameter. Additionally, the $p/q$-identifiability of specific graph families is investigated. These families include stars, double stars, and the graphs $K_1+e$, $K_2+e$, $P_2+2e$, and $P_3+2e$. The notions of $r_1/r_2$-identifiability for identifiable families of graphs and edges, as well as $r_1/r_2$-identifiability for families of graphs with a fixed diameter, are also explored. Ultimately, it is proven that for $p \ge 1$ and $q \ge 2$, the families of stars, double stars, and the aforementioned four graphs are $p/q$-identifiable precisely when their defining parameters satisfy certain conditions. These findings hold significant implications for the identification of graphs within the context of quantum error correcting codes. This study presents an initial measurement of the differential decay rate for the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^{+}\nu_{\mu}$ process. The analysis utilizes a dataset of 3.0/fb collected at the $\U(4978)^{0}$ resonance by the LHCb experiment at a center-of-mass energy of 10.02 TeV. By fitting the angular distribution of the reconstructed $D_s^{*0}$ meson, the form of the differential decay rate with respect to meson recoil is determined. The resulting angular distribution and differential decay rate align with theoretical predictions derived from the pole model and the quadratic extrapolation of the timelike pion and kaon differential scattering rates. Ultimately, no statistically significant preference was found for either the pole model or the extrapolation method in describing the observed angular distribution or the differential decay rate. This work employs a combination of the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*0}X^{0}$ and lepton number conservation variables to constrain the background. The findings regarding the differential decay rate and its form are illustrated through tables and figures. The described approach could potentially be applied to other semi-leptonic decays to extract further physics parameters. This research was conducted by the LHCb collaboration.

This study investigates the nonlinear dynamics responsible for the intermittent, crackling acoustic emissions generated when peeling an adhesive strip under a fixed pulling speed. By analyzing the force-time and acceleration-time traces, we identified specific nonlinear features indicative of crack formation. Concurrently, we defined two structural parameters: the inter-event interval (III), representing the duration between successive slip events, and the concealed event ratio (CER), which quantifies the proportion of III attributed to undetected events. Our findings reveal a power-law dependence of both the III and CER on the pulling speed, accompanied by the emergence of distinct event types. These results support a model featuring two dominant inter-event intervals and corresponding event categories, driven by the competition between shear stress buildup and stress release at the crack tip. Furthermore, we observed a linear relationship between the CER and the acoustic energy release rate, a connection that could prove valuable for seismic applications. The identified nonlinear characteristics and derived parameters offer significant insights for understanding delamination failures in engineering structures and earthquakes in geophysical contexts. Specifically, introducing the CER provides a method to assess the extent of undetected events within an inter-event, a critical factor for seismic hazard evaluation. To facilitate this research, an open-source Python code for extracting event details from acoustic emission data is available at https://github.com/rajivkumar1980/Concealed-Events. In 1921/22, K. Menger introduced the concept of an abstract metric space and proposed a comprehensive theory of metric spaces equipped with an angular function, which he termed "linear spaces." He also investigated the embeddability of such spaces into Euclidean spaces. Concurrently, Menger attempted to define an angular function within a generalized geometry encompassing Euclidean, Minkowski, and non-Euclidean hyperbolic varieties. He formulated two problems concerning the characterization of Euclidean spaces by means of this angular function and the realization of Euclidean metric spaces as "linear spaces," assuming the metric could be reconstructed from the angle. Although these efforts were significant, certain definitions and assertions required refinement. This paper revisits the works of Menger and other scholars on metric and angular spaces, addressing specific shortcomings in earlier formulations. We offer precise definitions for the metric and angular functions, along with a revised characterization of the Euclidean metric from which the Euclidean distance can be recovered. Furthermore, we correct certain statements in [3,4,6,7] and establish a new characterization of Euclidean metric spaces that allows the metric itself to be embedded. Our approach relies on a generalization of the law of cosines, which we derive for spaces endowed with an angular function and a compatible metric. Our findings indicate that both of Menger's problems possess negative solutions. Nevertheless, we provide a comprehensive theory of metric and Euclidean spaces that utilize an angle function, a compatible metric, and an embedding of the metric—structures that extend the traditional definition of an Euclidean space by incorporating an explicit Euclidean metric. We conclude with several open questions. Our results demonstrate that, aside from the necessity of a genuine Euclidean metric, no other obstacles exist to treating Minkowski and hyperbolic spaces as Euclidean-like spaces with an associated angular function and a compatible metric. Consequently, the term "linear space" introduced by Menger in 1921/22 is no longer required. Our framework applies universally to all spaces featuring an metric and an angle function, offering a unified treatment for Euclidean, Minkowski, and hyperbolic varieties. This work serves as a sequel to [10], where the authors defined an information-theoretic measure of curvature for metric spaces with an angular function and demonstrated that Euclidean, Minkowski, and hyperbolic spaces achieve minimal, maximal, and intermediate values, respectively. Furthermore, this paper supersedes the study by A. Khan and the first author

Neural network-based point cloud representations have achieved significant success in recent years. However, training these models requires a massive volume of labeled data, which is often difficult to acquire. To address this limitation, we introduce TPC, a framework that enables neural representations to leverage traditional transformation-dependent filters, such as FFT and SOON. By integrating these filters into the processing pipeline, TPC allows point clouds to utilize established traditional deep learning architectures like ResNet and EfficientNet for classification. Crucially, our approach dynamically selects the appropriate filter based on the specific transformation—rotation, scaling, or translation—applied to the coordinates before classification. Extensive experiments conducted on two standard datasets, ModelNet40 and ShapeNetPart, demonstrate that TPC outperforms existing methods, including our own neural smoothing technique. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ShapeGroups/TPC.

This study introduces a novel approach to determine the precise shape of inclusions within self-sensing composite materials via electrical impedance tomography. Unlike conventional methods that rely on predefined inclusion shapes, this technique enables the passive detection of crack shapes in functionally graded carbon fiber-reinforced polymer composites with in-plane anisotropic damage conductivity tensors. To achieve this, an exact global optimization method based on a genetic algorithm is employed to identify the shape of inclusions with elliptical symmetry. The proposed strategy was applied to detect the shape of a through-the-crack in a self-sensing carbon fiber-reinforced polymer composite. The results confirm that the method successfully identifies the crack's exact shape, with an average shape error of 0.0013. Furthermore, the approach effectively distinguishes between the opening and through-the depths of the crack. These findings indicate that this method can detect the exact shape of inclusions with simple geometries, such as cracks, without requiring any a priori assumptions about the geometry itself. Consequently, this passive shape detection method offers significant advantages over traditional techniques, which typically approximate crack shapes using combinations of simple geometric elements like circles, ellipses, or polygons. The proposed exact global optimization method for identifying inclusion shapes holds potential for applications in damage identification, electrical impedance tomography, and other inverse problems involving self-sensing composites. Ultimately, integrating this inclusion shape detection method with a recent self-sensing composite damage identification technique could yield a comprehensive solution for fully characterizing the topology of complex crack topologies. Regarding nomenclature, the term "inclusion" is used here to describe regions with altered electrical conductivity tensors, encompassing both cracks and other conductivity anomalies. For the specific case of a through-the-crack, the methodology successfully identified its exact geometry, including its length and orientation.

This study introduces geometric metrics for evaluating tensor-based Euclidean space representations. Furthermore, the authors define a "closeness" metric to compare these representations against a reference hypercontraction tensor, ultimately establishing an optimal representation for Euclidean areas and volumes. Finally, the concept of a "simplex" is extended from standard geometry to the tensor representation of Euclidean areas.

High-dimensional matrix inversion is essential for numerous scientific and engineering domains, yet it remains computationally demanding. While recent literature introduced an iterative method to accelerate inversion via approximation, it relied on a limited technique for reducing matrix order. This paper generalizes that method by employing a more comprehensive approach to matrix order reduction, yielding faster iterative inversion. Additionally, we expand the application of this approach beyond square matrices to encompass rectangular matrices. Although this generalization of the iterative method of record requires approximately 2.5 times more iterations to reach a specified accuracy, the combined effect of reduced computational complexity per iteration and the generalized order reduction technique results in a significant overall speedup. Furthermore, when implemented on a GPU, this approach delivers an additional performance gain of roughly an order of magnitude compared to GPU execution of the previous method. The generalized technique is particularly beneficial for applications involving very large matrices where a low-rank approximation is acceptable, enabling the use of a prolonged iterative process to achieve high-dimensional inversion. To facilitate this, we also provide a C++ open-source library containing the necessary routines. This library supports both square and rectangular matrices, as well as complex arithmetic, and is accessible at https://github.com/egnmr/HigherOrderInversion. We conclude with a discussion of potential future extensions.

Situational linear bandits represent a recently introduced model designed to address context-dependent decisions in human learning and artificial intelligence. This model finds significant applications in education, where the goal is to determine optimal teaching strategies for specific learning contexts, and in advertising, where the aim is to select the most effective advertisement for a given user. In this work, we investigate learning in a distributed situational linear bandit scenario from a nonparametric perspective. Specifically, an agent operating in a target context seeks to minimize regret by interacting with an expert located in a source context. Crucially, the target agent has no access to the source context and cannot observe the target context's situations prior to learning. We establish a lower bound for this learning problem and propose a novel algorithm that achieves the optimal regret upper bound. Furthermore, we introduce a real-world scenario to demonstrate the practical value of this research. The findings indicate that the optimal upper bound relies on three key factors: the dimension of the feature space in the target context, the dimension of the latent situational space, and the Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) norm of the regret function within the source context. This result is particularly significant because it shows that learning can occur in the target context without dependence on the feature dimension of the source context. Ultimately, this work highlights the potential of nonparametric methods for solving contextual learning problems across distributed environments.

This study conducts linear stability analyses to examine how dust development influences the vertical shear instability (VSI) in the outer zones of protoplanetary disks. The analysis reveals that the VSI growth rate initially increases with rising dust concentration due to enhanced thermal diffusion. However, beyond a specific threshold, the growth rate declines as gas turbulence is suppressed by the dust. Furthermore, the vertical scale over which VSI instabilities develop expands with higher dust concentrations. These findings suggest that local dust formation can amplify VSI activity in the external regions of protoplanetary disks. Consequently, the VSI may contribute to the accretion-driven heating observed in these areas, offering a solution to the heating mechanism puzzle when dust is present. Ultimately, this work highlights the critical role of dust in the linear growth phase of vertical shear instabilities within protoplanetary disks. Linear stability analyses are performed using a simplified model that incorporates dust evolution, while the resulting growth rates are validated against direct simulations of VSI involving dust. It is anticipated that future research will explore the implications of these linear findings on the overall evolution of these disks. Such investigations will be detailed in the companion paper by Fromang \& Flock (2019). Additionally, this study assumes that the Rossby Kelvin-Helmholtz instability (RHKHI) does not occur in the outer regions, as the rotation rates required for its onset are unlikely when dust accumulation suppresses rotation profiles. This assumption will also be addressed in the forthcoming companion work.

This study establishes a Liouville theorem on the Riemannian manifold $M$, which is a $\nicefrac{1}{2}$-Ricci diminutive manifold possessing constant scalar curvature, where the Laplacian of the scalar curvature is bounded from above. The proof relies on Li and Yau's gradient estimate for harmonic functions on complete Riemannian manifolds satisfying $Ricci \geq 0$ and Chen's Liouville theorem regarding harmonic functions with specific gradient and Hessian constraints. As applications, we demonstrate that no stable minimal immersion exists from parabolic manifolds into constant curvature manifolds, and we derive a rigidity result for minimal manifolds with constant mean curvature (cmc) immersed into constant curvature spaces. Furthermore, we introduce a variational approach to prove additional rigidity theorems for cmc manifolds within constant curvature environments.

This paper introduces Global Mean Pooling (GMP) as a replacement for dynamic entrance layers in Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) designed for video classification tasks. By substituting the GMP layer for the initial frame pooling operation, the model gains the ability to process videos of variable lengths without requiring a fixed dimension. The proposed architecture, termed GMP-Net, eliminates the need for dynamic layers, thereby simplifying the network structure and enhancing computational efficiency. Extensive experiments conducted on two public datasets, UCF-101 and HMDB-51, confirm that GMP-Net outperforms existing state-of-the methods. Furthermore, the model demonstrates robustness when trained and tested on videos of differing lengths. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/GMP-Net. Ultimately, this work offers a novel perspective on handling videos of variable duration through the GMP layer, which holds significant potential for future research.
