This study introduces Random Stroll for Education (RfE), a novel approach to model training for Federated Learning (FL) systems serving clients with non-independent and identically distributed (NIDID) data. By leveraging a lightweight data exploration algorithm, RfE enables a central model to learn from data volumes that would otherwise be insufficient for individual clients. The combination of the data exploration algorithm and the central model constitutes an Educated Model (EM). Unlike the traditional model updated at the conclusion of each iteration, the EM is updated at every step to guide the selection of local training data for each client. We evaluated RfE using the English Language Learning (ELL) dataset, a real-world scenario involving students accessing an educational mobile application. The results indicate that for the specific ELL dataset, the Random Stroll algorithm effectively identifies high-quality data, and the RfE method achieves superior accuracy compared to standard data sampling techniques. Furthermore, RfE significantly reduces the data processing time per iteration for each client. These findings suggest that Random Stroll is an effective data exploration strategy for similar datasets, offering a viable solution to expand training data for underrepresented samples and enhancing the performance of educational models within FL environments. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Aniruddha1999/RfE.

This paper introduces an uncomplicated consistency regularization method designed to enhance the performance of pixel-level semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed approach leverages both labeled and unlabeled data, utilizing a small collection of supervised images for training and a larger set of unsupervised images for prediction. It combines a segmentation network with a classification network to create a two-stage framework. During training, the segmentation model generates pixel-wise maps from the unlabeled images, which are then fed into the classifier. Conversely, the segmentation network is guided by the classifier's predictions on those same images. To optimize both models across the labeled and unlabeled datasets, we employ mean squared error (MSE) loss for the supervised images and a consistency loss for the unsupervised ones. Experiments conducted on two public medical image datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms existing techniques. Furthermore, the incorporation of classification-based consistency regularization significantly improves the performance of the segmentation network on the unlabeled data. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/An-Awkwardly-Basic-Consistency-Regularization-Technique-For-Some-Pixel-Level-Semi-Supervised-Healthcare-Image-Segmentation-Using-End-To-End-Attention-U-Net-And-ResNet-50. Guidance, the mechanism enabling Bohmian trajectories, represents a form of nonlocality that has been demonstrated through various nonminimal models, including the pilot-wave model, Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen (EPR) steering, and Bell nonlocality. We establish that nonlocal guidance arises from the nonlocality of the single-particle wave function, which in turn stems from entanglement between the particle's position and momentum. Consequently, any source of single-particle entanglement can generate nonlocality. We specifically investigate single-particle entanglement caused by orbital angular momentum (OAM) mode superposition, showing that it produces nonlocality and enabling its verification via a Bell test. Furthermore, we confirm that OAM nonlocality and nonlocal guidance are mutually dependent on the degree of OAM mode nonorthogonality. Ultimately, we introduce a protocol to generate genuine single-particle entanglement on demand, thereby creating nonlocality and nonlocal guidance as required. This achievement constitutes the first demonstration of a genuine nonlocal resource, which we term "single-particle entanglement," capable of producing nonlocal effects analogous to how EPR entanglement yields bipartite nonlocal effects. Our findings reveal that single-particle entanglement serves as the origin of both nonlocal guidance and the "bunching" of Bohmian trajectories observed in interference experiments. These results also clarify the source of apparent nonlocality in recent experiments utilizing OAM superpositions, which fall short of true nonlocality due to the inherent nonorthogonality of specific OAM modes. We conclude by outlining potential applications of single-particle entanglement. This article is accompanied by a Video of the Supplementary Material [1] and three additional figures.

This study introduces an algorithm and hardware co-development framework for energy-efficient LSTM networks used in video recognition tasks. We propose a novel hardware architecture capable of executing both forward and tensor decomposition operations. Consequently, we introduce a two-stage method for creating energy-optimized, high-performance LSTM networks: first, optimizing the network structure using a gradient-based approach, and second, applying tensor decomposition for further efficiency. To validate this approach, we developed a collection of LSTM models with varying levels of structural optimization and tensor decomposition. The results demonstrate that a model achieving 90\% accuracy on the YouTube-Faces dataset required only 100MFLOPs per frame and 0.7MB of memory, representing a 10x reduction in computational load and a 5x decrease in memory usage compared to a model with identical accuracy but no tensor decomposition. When deployed on our custom hardware, this optimized model operated at 1.0GHz with a power consumption of 0.7W. Furthermore, based on the findings from structural and tensor-level optimizations, we derived a new theoretical framework for decomposing high-order tensors. Finally, we implemented this framework in PyTorch to convert a state-of-the-art model on the YouTube-Faces dataset, reducing its order by 2 and resulting in a 1.5x improvement in both accuracy and power efficiency.

This study examines the Schr\"odinger equation defined within the exterior of a convex barrier, subject to a nonlinear Neumann boundary condition. We demonstrate that the solution may experience an explosion (singularity formation) when the system's initial energy surpasses a specific threshold. Furthermore, we establish global existence for initial conditions characterized by low energy. These findings extend previous results, which had only addressed explosions in the context of the Schr\"odinger equation on a half-plane with a focusing power-type nonlinear boundary condition.

Hypothesis testing in statistics relies on two primary methodologies: p-values and Bayes factors. While the scientific community has long advocated for Bayes factors as a complement to significance testing, their practical application has been limited. This limitation stems from the widespread belief that Bayes factors are overly sensitive to prior choices, a characteristic that appears to contradict their goal of offering an objective measure of evidence. In this paper, we challenge this assumption, arguing that Bayes factors can be employed more effectively if specific strategies are adopted regarding both the selection of priors and the computation of the factors themselves. Achieving these goals requires a tailored approach. We begin by clarifying the source of the sensitivity problem and outlining the necessary conditions for its resolution. Subsequently, we introduce two distinct strategies for incorporating domain knowledge into the priors used for effect size parameters within the calculation of Bayes factors. Furthermore, we present two complementary methods for determining the remaining components of the Bayes factor—specifically, the prior predictive densities for the data under each hypothesis. Finally, we detail two computational frameworks for calculating Bayes factors: a direct method and an indirect method, with the latter involving the estimation of effect sizes. Through a series of examples, we demonstrate how these strategies and methods function in practice. These applications also highlight the importance of carefully considering the prior distribution of the Bayes factor itself, which serves as the denominator when computing the evidence. By the end of this work, readers will be equipped with a set of strategies and techniques designed to maximize the utility of Bayes factors for evaluating the evidence supporting data under a given hypothesis. It is important to note, however, that these approaches are specifically intended for scientific investigations aiming to assess the strength of evidence for or against hypotheses; they should not be applied when selecting between statistically identical models based on other criteria, such as optimizing predictive performance. Regarding the use of Bayesian inference for parameter estimation, this is unnecessary for calculating Bayes factors when employing the indirect method, as the prior predictive distribution of the effect size is utilized rather than its posterior distribution. Nevertheless, selecting an appropriate method for this step is crucial for ensuring efficient computation. Discourse indicators, also referred to as connectives, function as linguistic markers that supply information regarding the semantic and syntactic connections between clauses or sentences. Although recent years have seen substantial progress in the manual creation of resources for specific indicator types to support tasks like classification and classification-plus, these initiatives have predominantly concentrated on singular types. This study introduces a resource designed to examine all discourse indicators within a corpus and introduces an automated method for validating the semantic categories assigned to these indicators. Applying this approach to the Wall Street Journal portion of the Penn Treebank, we identified 339 unique indicators, a figure that aligns closely with the 329 types outlined in the recent comprehensive taxonomy by Vlachos and Riedel. Utilizing a taxonomy-aware neural model, we determined that this specific corpus is insufficient to fully cover the taxonomy; consequently, we expanded our analysis to the larger LUDBCRE corpus, identifying 509 distinct indicators. Our findings indicate that the initial resource, dubbed DiscIndIndr, offers a valuable complement to existing discourse indicators frameworks and can assist in guiding the development of taxonomies and related resources for specific indicator types. Furthermore, we presented an automated technique for assessing the quality of these indicators and their associated categories, a tool that can be employed to evaluate the efficacy of future specialized initiatives. Access to both resources and the discourse indicators indicator (DIndIndr) is available at https://github.com/rohitgupta1999/DiscIndIndr. The discourse indicators plus taxonomy (DiscIndIndr+) resource can be obtained from the authors. Furthermore, the classifier used to generate this resource (ClassIndIndr) serves as a useful component for downstream applications, such as a meaningful discourse classification task (DiscClass+). This paper addresses the challenge of deciding inclusion between deterministic finite automata and expressions defined by a regular language grammar. Specifically, we provide a novel, fully symbolic, and compositional solution for resolving inequalities involving extended regular expressions. Our approach integrates a new prioritized, sound, and complete completion method with a term simplification strategy based on a simplified regular grammar. Unlike existing solutions that rely on backtracking and regression, our method operates without regression. We validate the effectiveness of our approach through the resolution of numerous open cases from the literature and via comparisons with state-of-the-art automated reasoning systems. The proposed technique has been implemented in the source library of the Coq proof assistant. Additionally, this work serves as the foundational proof component for establishing zero knowledge proofs for regular expression leakage in cryptographic protocols within the CORe library.

In the context of the AdS$_{3}$/CFT$_{2}$ correspondence, we examine the classical equation governing the 4-point function of global $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ operators on the cylinder, which arises from the boundary integral of the 4-point function on $SL(2,\mathbb{R})\times SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ (global coordinates). This equation consists of two distinct parts: the product of global operator 4-point function and a boundary integral of an OPE segment rotation Wigner function, and a second term representing the rotation of a 4-point boundary integral OPE segment. We demonstrate that incorporating a specific linear combination of the 4-point boundary integral functions into the boundary integral of the 4-point global operator function yields a recursive relation. This relation allows for the computation of the boundary integral of a $s$-point OPE segment rotation Wigner function using a combination of boundary integrals of an $(s+1)$-point OPE segment rotation Wigner function and an $(s+1)$-point boundary integral. Furthermore, we derive a recursion for the bulk integral of an $s$-point OPE segment rotation, expressing it as a combination of the bulk integral of an $(s+1)$-point OPE segment rotation and an boundary integral of an $(s+1)$-point boundary OPE segment. Leveraging a recent result by Fitzpatrick, Kaplan, and Wang [12] regarding the bulk integral of a 3-point OPE segment rotation, we establish recursion relations for both the boundary and bulk integrals of a 3-point OPE segment rotation. Finally, we derive a closed-form expression for the boundary integral of a 4-point OPE segment rotation and validate it numerically.

This study introduces a novel architecture for lobster-eye X-ray telescopes, designed to expand both the field of view and effective area beyond the constraints of current systems. This new configuration utilizes a multiplexed arrangement of smaller lobster-eye modules, each equipped with a conventional imaging zone plate at its focal plane to record a compact, high-resolution image of a specific sky sector. The concept is detailed through simulations of a monitor serving a 20,000 square degree field, composed of nine 2,200 square degree sectors. Simulation outcomes indicate that a 90\% field of view with a resolution of 10 arcminutes can be achieved across the 18,000 square degree area covered by the nine modules. Furthermore, the angular resolution within the central field of view of each module can be enhanced to approximately 5 arcminutes by optimizing the interplay between the lobster-eye lens and the imaging zone plate. These simulations confirm that multiplexing lobster-eye lenses is feasible and offers a viable method for broad-field monitoring with uniform resolution. Such a system would be particularly valuable for post-outburst multi-variable observations, enabling rapid identification of variable sources and the rapid deployment of narrow-field instruments to investigate the event's field. Potential applications include rapid response to X-ray transients detected by wide-field monitors like NEUTRON Star X-ray INstrument (NIXI) on the IXPE satellite or the Imager for X-ray Astrophysics Satellite (IXAS) on the STIXI satellite, as well as pre- and post-event observations of astronomical phenomena by other telescopes. Additionally, this multiplexed design could serve as an effective focal instrument for microgravity experiments aimed at characterizing various X-ray lens technologies. Feasibility simulations for this architecture are conducted using the open-source Monte Carlo ray-tracing code, GEANT4.9.x.

This study introduces a novel framework to investigate the impact of the cosmic speed field (CSF) on the dark matter halo (DMH) mass distribution. By employing machine learning techniques, we reconstructed the CSF from large-scale structure (LSS) using the BOSS DR12 CMB rest-frame spectroscopic data. The analysis reveals that the l=2 angular power spectrum of the reconstructed CSF aligns more closely with predictions from $\Lambda$CDM simulations than previously observed anisotropies in the BOSS DR12 data. Furthermore, the reconstructed DMH mass function (MF) derived from BOSS DR12 exhibits a significantly better match with the MF from the $\Lambda$CDM simulation compared to the traditional DMH MF obtained directly from the same spectroscopic data. These results indicate that previous discrepancies between the BOSS DR12 DMH MF and $\Lambda$CDM simulations were likely caused by measurement errors in the CSF within the spectroscopic data. Consequently, when extracting small-scale physical quantities from LSS data, it is essential to account for the previously underestimated stochasticity of the CSF. To achieve this, we developed a two-step neural network approach: first, a U-Net architecture was used to recover the speed field from the LLS, followed by a separate neural network that reconstructed the DMH mass from the BOSS DR12 data after correcting for velocity effects. Finally, we verified the consistency of the recovered DMH mass with theoretical predictions by utilizing other observable quantities, such as the luminosity function and clustering amplitude, within the BOSS DR12 dataset. The source code for this research is accessible at: https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/UNRVELING_CSF.

Detecting local magnetic field anomalies, such as those caused by Meissner expulsion, poses a significant challenge for atom interferometry due to the inherent sensitivity to uniform field gradients. This difficulty is particularly acute when measuring the gravitational constant ($G$) via atomic interferometry to address current discrepancies in the CODATA value of $G$. We demonstrate that a local magnetometer-based feedback mechanism enables the detection of local magnetic field changes previously beyond the reach of atomic interferometry. By leveraging a superconducting local shield, we successfully identified the local field alterations induced by a nearby superconducting sphere. Employing a Rubidium-87 atomic fountain interferometer, we conducted a proof-of-principle experiment to observe the gravitational attraction between two bulk superconductors. The results indicate that a local magnetic field of approximately $10^{-10}$ T can be detected with a 1-second integration time. Furthermore, we theoretically derived a sensitivity of $10^{-11}$ T for an integration time of 100,000 seconds. This study presents the initial proof that an atomic interferometer can detect local magnetic field variations by utilizing a superconducting local shield. Additionally, we proposed a method to measure gravitational anomalies arising from local magnetic fields, which could help identify such interference in future $G$ determination experiments using atomic interferometry. Ultimately, this work offers evidence for detecting local magnetic field-induced gravitational anomalies between two bulk superconductors via atomic interferometry. This study examines magnetic Mn adatoms and dimers situated on the Nb(110) surface using the framework of initial principles relativistic theory. Specifically, we analyze spin-dependent characteristics of electron wave functions, focusing on the anisotropy of spin currents flowing between the tip of a scanning tunneling microscope (STM) and the Mn adatoms/dimers when the tip is positioned above the Mn magnetic moments. The results indicate that spin currents are anisotropic with respect to the direction of tunneling; for instance, when the STM current aligns with the x-axis, the current measured with a positive bias voltage exceeds that with a negative voltage by approximately 10%, a phenomenon driven by the anisotropy of the wave function. Furthermore, the findings reveal that the initial vector model of magnetism fails to accurately represent the anisotropic nature of spin currents and wave functions in these systems. Finally, we report on the formation of a magnetic domain with a Néel-type structure when a positive bias voltage is applied between the STM tip and the sample.

This study introduces a novel framework for detecting skin cancer types using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and an outlier identification mechanism. The proposed architecture comprises three sequential modules: an initial ConvNet block, an outlier identification module, and a final ConvNet block responsible for classifying skin images into nine distinct categories. The outlier identification component employs a 1D ConvNet to generate a score reflecting the likelihood that an image is an anomaly. The first ConvNet block and the final classification block utilize a hybrid design combining standard convolutional layers with fully connected layers. Experimental results demonstrate that this architecture effectively identifies nine different skin conditions, including various carcinomas, from publicly available datasets. Furthermore, the outlier identification module successfully recognizes anomalous images that were misclassified by conventional models, as well as samples with labels differing from their actual categories. These findings indicate that the integrated framework of the initial ConvNet block, the outlier detection component, and the final classification block performs superiorly compared to existing methods. At forward high-energy $p-p$ collisions, $W$ and $Z$ bosons are produced via Drell-Yan processes and subsequently interact with the opposite proton, giving rise to LLeV (Lepton-Leading Weak Boson) events. These are valuable for investigating elastic and diffractive $W/Z-p$ scattering. Given that the incoming muon carries a large unknown transverse momentum, detectors with limited granularity and rapidity coverage face significant challenges in reconstructing the missing $p_T$ to measure differential cross-sections. To address this, we introduce a new method for determining the missing $p_T$ with high precision using the lepton's angular distribution. This approach enables the construction of differential cross-sections with respect to $p_T$ and $M_{\ell\ell}$. Furthermore, to facilitate access to ultra-high luminosity needed for these differential measurements, we propose utilizing beams with a small crossing angle, a technique already implemented at the LHC for Higgs-strahlung studies. Employing Monte Carlo simulations, we demonstrate that this technique delivers superior resolution compared to the standard method, which relies on the hadronic missing $p_T$ derived from calorimeter energy deposits. The proposed solution is also applicable to other processes involving charged-lepton final states, such as $\nu-p$ interactions. Ultimately, to achieve the required luminosity for these differential studies in proton-proton collisions, we outline a feasible configuration for future high-energy muon colliders.

Invariant curves play a crucial role in the qualitative analysis of dynamical systems, particularly when investigating the local stability of fixed points and the existence of invariant sets. This paper demonstrates that for specific families of fractional-order systems, neither the characteristic equation nor the system itself guarantees the presence of invariant lines or those with slopes other than unity. Furthermore, it is proven that no parabolic invariant surfaces exist within these same families. These findings offer new insights into the study of invariant sets for fractional-order systems and carry significant implications for their qualitative examination. Consequently, these results correct certain errors identified in previous research regarding fractional-order systems. Additionally, the approach outlined here provides a straightforward method for addressing similar problems in other systems. The validity of these conclusions is supported by both theoretical reasoning and numerical evidence.

This study addresses the inverse problem within a structural acoustic application, aiming to reconstruct the boundary excitation applied to a plate using interior acoustic field measurements. The reconstruction relies on an iterative iterative regularized least-squares method, supported by a priori information regarding the excitation's characteristics. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach can effectively recover boundary excitations that are both spatially and temporally complex. The findings hold significant potential for applications in noise source identification and nondestructive evaluation. Furthermore, this work represents the first attempt to resolve boundary excitation reconstruction through an inverse framework via a numerical iteration technique, distinguishing it from prior research that utilized dictionary learning for similar goals.

We introduce the simplest scoto-seesaw model extending the standard model, where both the neutrino seesaw mechanism and dark matter stability are ensured by a single additional scalar singlet and one new scalar triplet. We comprehensively examine the parameter space through the lens of dark matter phenomenology, neutrless double beta decay, Higgs production and decay rates, electroweak precision tests, electroweak scale stability, and various scalar vacuum robustness criteria. Our analysis reveals a hierarchy of regions based on the origin of neutrino mass: a type-I dominated area, followed by mixed type-I and type-III sections, and finally a type-III dominated region. Within the type-I dominated sector, we identify three distinct zones regarding WIMP detectability at direct detection experiments. We provide a detailed characterization of the viable parameter spaces across these various regions. Our findings indicate that the mixed type-I and type-III sector offers the most promising ground for future theoretical and experimental exploration. This region naturally accounts for the neutrino mass scale, remains compatible with all current experimental constraints, satisfies scalar vacuum robustness requirements, and can be probed via inverse neutrinoless double beta decay, direct dark matter detection, and future colliders. For the currently favored parameter points, the extra Higgs sector exhibits a characteristic pattern of tree-level vacuum stability: one heavy scalar is a local minimum, while two lighter scalars form a global minimum at large field values, a configuration necessitating the consideration of higher-dimensional operators for true vacuum robustness. We conclude by highlighting the unique theoretical attributes and testable predictions of this simplest scoto-seesaw framework.
